doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: Dizzy Gillespie, rhythm over note choice, and hearing the upbeats
summary: After a week touring with Dizzy, Galper focused on rhythm and upbeats, mentions Mike Longo's DVDs, and hears a Miles solo from the offbeat side.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: So you do A, you do A2, you’re expecting A3 but you just take a little bit of A2 and go off with it and next thing you know you’ve got a line. And it takes off and it has a life of its own. It’s almost magical. I had the good fortune to spend a week with Dizzy Gillespie when he was a guest for Phil’s band. We toured a week with him. I was never the same after that. Dizzy totally turned me around to realize the rhythmic basis, he said, “Hal, Bird invented the melodies, I invented the rhythm.” And his legacy, Mike Longo, you’re familiar with Mike Longo — he just passed away. He’s the one that has been preserving Dizzy’s rhythmic legacy. He’s got three DVDs out that are mind-blowing about the rhythm. And since my time with Dizzy I’ve been focusing almost exclusively on rhythm. Not note choice. Because what happens is the music’s going by too fast to choose notes tone by tone. But the rhythm has pressure to it and the rhythm presses you into action. It’s called selective pressure. I’m not explaining myself well. It’s too big a subject for me to sit here and talk about it, it would take up all this time. Okay so say you play a first note. How do you decide your second note? What decides the second note? The rhythm. You have 496 million possibilities of the chromatic scale within the octave. How do you pick the second note? You know? That was the question. It’s done through surprise. It’s done unexpected. You break a pattern, it needs to be solved. The brain has a natural intensity to seek equilibrium all the time. Something wrong happens to the body it immediately starts working to get equilibrium. It cannot stand tension, it wants to resolve tension. When you create — that’s tension-release, tension-release. That’s the whole process right there. A and B. It’s an amazing concept. I don’t have the scientific underpinnings to back it up but it works. And you’re right, I have opinions but I’m one of the last of the apprenticeship system. So the stuff that I’m talking about I’ve experienced and I just happen to have the facility luckily to be able to talk about it well but — what can I — the rhythmic part of the thing — like Dizzy said the more upbeats in the music the more it swings. And there’s a tremendous concern about how musicians deal with the upbeat these days, because they don’t know how to deal with it. And Barry Harris used to talk about it, Dizzy talked about it. Dizzy said, “Well if the quarter notes are a continuum then the upbeats have to be a continuum.” So I don’t know, wait a minute. So I’ve been working on feeling the beat as a shuffle [scats] try to get it that way. Try to figure out ways to deal with it.
I think a shuffle is the most entrancing beat that — it just like. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

Yeah. But I’m feeling it on the off-beats, not the downbeats. And what’s interesting is there’s a whole nother world on the offbeat side. It’s just a completely different world. Things sound completely different. I didn’t realize this but I was at my old lady’s loft a few months ago and she had put on Miles’ “Relaxin’” album, which was mother’s milk to me when I was young so I knew every solo by heart. And I’m listening to this Miles solo but I realized I was listening to it from the offbeat/upbeat side of the beat. And it sounded completely different. I never heard it that way in my life, which makes me realize I haven’t been hearing what I’ve been hearing correctly all or most of my life.
Do you think Miles — how do I ask this?
He comes out of Dizzy. You know he got it from Dizzy.

Dizzy was the one — and Mike Longo, the work he’s done in preserving his legacy is just mind blowing, historic, should be preserved, and those DVDs should be on every jazz musician’s shelf. There’s stuff on there I never heard of. Moody’s triplet. Moody’s triplets. I still don’t understand, even though Mike explained it. You know.
